title: Warmup Chaos & Boundary Probing — Stability Notes
content:
Purpose:
This note collects an experimental harness and methodology for exercising serving-runtime warmup behavior under small, deliberate disruptions — "chaos" — and for probing boundary conditions that reveal brittle paths in throughput and cache priming. The goal is not to find peak QPS, but to characterize repeatability envelopes and failure surfaces so automated benchmarks and SLAs are trustworthy.

Background and rationale:
- Our standard throughput runs are stable for steady traffic, but subtle ordering and priming differences produce large variance across runs when caches, batching, and kernel selection change.
- Typical artifacts: oscillations after node drains, slow tail latencies after periods of burst traffic, and throughput regression after deterministic-seed drift.
- Injecting small perturbations during warmup exposes brittle transitions (e.g., batching thresholds, KV cache cold-miss storms, quantized-kernel fallbacks).

High-level experiment goals:
1) Map regions of warmup duration and seed variability that yield <5% run-to-run throughput variance.
2) Identify minimal chaos injections that flip batching behavior or kernel selection.
3) Produce a compact repeatability checklist and a canonical run command for CI that tolerates realistic noise.

Test harness components (what to run):
- Load generator: support for configurable arrival patterns (poisson, staircase, constant), per-request sequence length distribution, token-batching aware clients, and deterministic RNG seeds.
- Chaos injector: network latency jitter, ephemeral CPU contention on select nodes, simulated node “drain” event, random model-variant fallback toggles, GPU power cap toggles (where supported).
- Observability hooks: request correlation-id propagation, span-level traces for batching/kvcache hits, GPU telemetry (util, mem), kernel selection logs, and server-side sampling of request inputs for repro.

Loadgen config guidelines (recommended knobs):
- arrival_pattern: use poisson for realistic variance and staircase for controlled ramp experiments.
- concurrency_sweep: [4, 8, 16, 32, 64] (adjust for hardware).
- seq_len_dist: provide a 3-point histogram (short/medium/long) with explicit weights.
- token_payloads: reuse a seed bank of 100 canonical prompts (sha'd) to preserve tokenization determinism.
- rng_seed: record and report; runs should be repeatable with the same seed and dataset.

Warmup strategies to compare:
- steady-primer: run constant low QPS (10–20% target) for X minutes to populate kv cache, then step to target.
- staircase-primer: quick staircase ramp (10→50→100% in steps) to exercise batching transitions and kernel selection.
- randomized-primer: random short bursts interleaved with idle gaps to stress boundary recovery.
- hybrid: short steady primer followed by staircase.

Chaos injection matrix (examples):
- network_jitter: add 20–200ms jitter on 1–2% of traffic during warmup window.
- node_drain: remove one serving node for 30–120s mid-warmup to force reroute and rebalance.
- cpu_burst: spawn CPU-hog on worker for 60s to see latency spillover into scheduling.
- gpu_powercap: reduce GPU TDP by 10–30% and observe kernel fallback latencies.
- seed_shift: change loadgen rng_seed halfway through warmup to simulate dataset drift.

Repeatability controls and seeding discipline:
- Always snapshot and commit: loadgen seed, prompt bank checksum, model version, quantization profile, hardware SKU, kernel override flags.
- Use deterministic tokenization: pin tokenizer version and report token counts per prompt.
- Anchor runs: for each experimental run save a small “anchor” short-run with a fixed micro-workload so posthoc comparisons are aligned.
- Multiple repeats: perform N>=5 repeats per cell and compute IQR in addition to mean.

Key metrics to capture (must be machine-readable timestamps):
- throughput_tokens_per_sec (aggregate and per-node)
- request_rate_rps (observed)
- latency_ms (p50, p90, p95, p99)
- tail_error_rate (5xx/timeout)
- avg_batch_size and batch_size_histogram
- kv_cache_hit_rate and cold_miss_storm_events
- kernel_selection_changes (count of different kernels used)
- GPU_util_pct, GPU_mem_used_mb
- process_cpu_pct and system_load
- queue_depths and request_queue_latency_ms

Observability and instrumentation notes:
- Tag every request with experiment_id and run_seed; propagate to traces and exporter.
- Emit an event stream for chaos injections (timestamped) so events correlate to metric perturbations.
- Capture a compact sampling of raw responses when anomalies occur (only prompts' sha and response signature to respect privacy).

Experiment matrix and scheduling (suggested):
- Dimensions: arrival_pattern x concurrency x primer_type x chaos_type x seq_len_profile x run_seed
- Start with a 12-cell smoke matrix (2 arrival patterns x 3 conc levels x 2 primer types) with no chaos to establish baseline variance.
- Expand to include single-chaos injections (one dimension at a time).
- For full characterization, run pairwise chaos combinations for cells that showed >10% variance.

Post-run analysis checklist:
1) Validate anchors: compare anchor metrics to baseline; if anchors drift >3% rerun.
2) Compute run-to-run IQR and CV; mark cells with CV>8% for deeper forensics.
3) Correlate metric deltas with chaos events timeline and kernel selection changes.
4) Inspect sampled traces for batching edge cases (very small/large batches) and cold cache spikes.
5) Produce a concise table: cell, seed, median_throughput, p95_latency, variance_flag, probable_cause, next_action.

Common failure modes and mitigations (practical tips):
- Symptom: repeated cold-miss storms after short warmup.  Mitigation: lengthen steady-primer or inject a targeted priming step for largest-seq prompts.
- Symptom: oscillation in throughput after node rejoin.  Mitigation: add a short cooldown period and avoid mid-warmup drains in CI unless explicitly testing.
- Symptom: non-deterministic batch sizes across repeats.  Mitigation: fix the batcher seed and align client pacing to target latency headroom.
- Symptom: high p99 due to kernel fallback.  Mitigation: capture kernel selection logs and try a controlled run forcing the fallback path to reproduce.

CI / automation recommendations:
- Canonical CI run is a reduced cell: staircase primer + poisson traffic at a medium concurrency with a fixed seed and anchor verification.
- If CI anchors pass, allow nightly extended-matrix runs that include chaos injections and longer warmup durations.
- Fail CI only on reproducible anchor regressions (not single noisy cells).

Sample loadgen invocation (illustrative):
./loadgen --experiment-id=warmup-chaos-v1 --arrival=poisson --concurrency=16 --seq-hist=short:0.6,med:0.3,long:0.1 --seed=1773 --primer=staircase --primer-steps=10,30,100 --warmup=420 --report-anchor=true --trace-prefix=warmup-chaos-v1

Open questions and future probes:
- How sensitive is kernel-selection hysteresis to sequence-length distribution drift in multi-tenant workloads?
- Can we synthesize a minimal prompt set that primes all hot KV entries in <60s for our common models?
- What is the smallest chaos injection that reliably reproduces a flaky CI run observed in customer traffic?

Appendix: quick checklist for running a reproducible chaos-warmup cell:
- [ ] pin model artifact + quantization hash
- [ ] pin tokenizer and prompt bank checksum
- [ ] commit loadgen flags and seed to experiment metadata
- [ ] enable request-level tracing and anchor run export
- [ ] schedule N>=5 repeats and aggregate IQR
- [ ] attach chaos event log to metric export

Notes to self / TODOs:
- wire up a small Grafana dashboard template capturing the key metrics listed above for rapid triage. (Evan to pick this up)
- add a scripted helper to extract kernel-selection diffs between runs. (Marta)
- follow up with infra on safe GPU powercap injection options in the staging cluster. (Owen)

End of note.
